97696899.extract:
Natural Distinction Un-natural Selection is a concept that highlights the interplay between natural and artificial elements, and how human activities impact the natural world. It is often represented in artistic and fashion contexts, such as the Spring/Summer 2009 collection by British fashion designer Alexander McQueen.

The collection contrasted the beauty of the environment with the impact of human industry. The first phase of the collection used soft colours, organic motifs, and flowing lines to present an image of nature unspoiled by man. The second phase featured prints manipulated to represent the intervention of human industry on nature.

In a broader philosophical sense, natural selection is a mechanism of evolution where organisms better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and pass on their genes. This concept is often used to explain the evolution of species over time.

The term 'Natural Distinction Un-natural Selection' can be seen as a metaphor for the influence of human activities on the natural world, and the contrast between natural and artificial elements. This idea is not only relevant in the fashion industry but also in various fields such as environmental science, ecology, and philosophy.

_In order to find inspiration for his S/S 2009 collection ‘Natural Dis-Tinction Un-Natural Selection’ (which can be seen in full [here](http://www.gainsburyandwhiting.com/fashionshow/alexander-mcqueen/natural-dis-tinction-un-natural-selections_s-09)), the program notes stated that McQueen had been looking into the works of Darwin and his theory of evolution. This research was evident in the abundance of animal print in the collection as well as the warehouse location of the show which was lined with taxidermy animals ranging from polar bears to tigers. The show appeared to be divided into two halves – one of which depicted a life untouched by man and another which depicted man’s interference with nature, creating an overall commentary on man’s influence on evolution. The theme was not unusual for McQueen, and it is one that he would go on to visually discuss in more detail with his following two collections._

[![Image 1](https://31.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_m9l29272Gd1qj7piio1_500.jpg)](https://31.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_m9l29272Gd1qj7piio1_500.jpg)

_Despite the serious nature of the show’s subject matter the designer stated that his intention was ‘not to preach’ – an intention which became clear when the clothing was unveiled. The silhouettes were all signature McQueen and the runway was awash with animal prints of all varieties as well as some subtle variations. The looks also showed technical precision and the sense that you were getting more for your money; for example, a closer look at a pink floral shift revealed flowers trapped beneath nude chiffon whereas silk evening jackets were nipped and tucked in various places to create animalistic proportions. The steel drums and tribal chants of the soundtrack were the perfect accompaniment to the first half of the show which felt like a walk through a beautiful jungle – silks were screenprinted with tiny yellow florals and loops of fabric moved with the models to give the impression of a bird in flight, whereas vibrant pink flamingos adorned sharply-tailored miniskirts and the exaggerated proportions of strapless minidresses created a series of makeshift exoskeletons._

[![Image 2](https://31.media.tumblr.com/55706f22919ec931e3b6d74e9e7577d4/tumblr_mpdb4oxggQ1rmn0b3o1_500.jpg)](https://31.media.tumblr.com/55706f22919ec931e3b6d74e9e7577d4/tumblr_mpdb4oxggQ1rmn0b3o1_500.jpg)

_The second half of the show was darker, just nowhere near as dark as we would expect from a mind so grotesque as that of McQueen. The colour palette started to shift into inkier hues and black crystal jumpsuits began to crop up alongside crystallised portraits of the iconic McQueen skull. The show’s invitation even bore the image that would soon be used as the cover of the ‘Savage Beauty’ exhibition book, a lenticular image which blended a photo of the designer’s face with that of a skeleton. Despite the beauty to be found in pieces such as the zip-lined leather cocoon dress or the grey python-print blazers, there was the sense that McQueen was holding back with his imagery._

[![Image 3](https://24.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_lt7xt37uun1qmifsro1_500.jpg)](https://24.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_lt7xt37uun1qmifsro1_500.jpg)

_The previous season was the first in which the fashion house had announced any profitability, and this collection seemed to pull a few punches for the sake of commercial appeal. The designs were typically stunning but there were a few missteps and certain ideas which felt they could have been pushed further. McQueen is renowned for his ambitious staging and overwhelmingly beautiful showpieces, so in this sense the show felt like less like a spectacle and more than a vague introduction to the two collections that would follow. The concept was meaty and there was plenty to discuss, but McQueen the businessman seemed reluctant to delve deep for fear of losing profit._

[![Image 4](https://24.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_lyuj1l96u01qgqq8eo1_500.gif)](https://24.media.tumblr.com/tumblr_lyuj1l96u01qgqq8eo1_500.gif)

1.title: Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection
1.content:
[![Image 1: Two mannequin dresses with skull and spinal cord print, one with an uneven hem and the other a sheath style](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/McQueen%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_des_beaux-arts_-_39.jpg/250px-McQueen%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_des_beaux-arts_-_39.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:McQueen,_Mus%C3%A9e_des_beaux-arts_-_39.jpg)

Digitally-printed minidresses from the collection presented at the _Alexander McQueen: Mind, Mythos, Muse_ exhibition at [Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_national_des_beaux-arts_du_Qu%C3%A9bec "Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec"), 2023

_**Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection**_ is the thirty-third collection by British fashion designer [Alexander McQueen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McQueen "Alexander McQueen"), released for the Spring/Summer 2009 season of his [eponymous fashion house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McQueen_(brand) "Alexander McQueen (brand)"). The collection reflected McQueen's concerns about [human impact on the environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_impact_on_the_environment "Human impact on the environment"), while drawing inspiration from the work of naturalist [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin "Charles Darwin"). _Natural Dis-tinction_ is known for its pioneering use of digital prints, which were engineered to match the [patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern_(sewing) "Pattern (sewing)") of their garments.

Two distinct phases of designs contrasted the beauty of the environment with the impact of human industry. The first phase used soft colours, organic motifs, and flowing lines to present an image of nature unspoiled by man. The second featured prints manipulated to look unnaturally perfect, with some designs in artificially bright colours and others in black and white. Across both phases, McQueen presented both classical and experimental silhouettes. Forty-one looks were presented at the collection's [runway show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway_show "Runway show"), which was staged on 3 October 2008 at the [Cent Quatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent_Quatre "Cent Quatre") building in Paris, a community centre that was once a [mortuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortuary "Mortuary"). The catwalk was framed by two lines of exotic [taxidermy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxidermy "Taxidermy") animals; a large round screen at the rear of the stage showed projections of celestial bodies and McQueen's own eyeball.

Contemporary critical response was somewhat mixed, with journalists preferring the more romantic first half of the show. Some were disappointed at the lack of runway theatrics for which McQueen had been known. McQueen continued to explore environmental themes and digital prints in his following two collections; he is credited with popularising the use of such prints in fashion. Ensembles from _Natural Dis-tinction_ are held by various museums and have appeared in exhibitions such as the McQueen retrospective _[Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander\_McQueen:\_Savage\_Beauty "Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty")_.

British fashion designer [Alexander McQueen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McQueen "Alexander McQueen") was known for his imaginative, sometimes controversial designs, and dramatic [fashion shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion_show "Fashion show").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1723-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoraBerry2022126,_128,_132-2) During his nearly twenty-year career, he explored a broad range of ideas and themes, including [historicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicism_(art) "Historicism (art)"), [romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism"), femininity, sexuality, and death.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1723-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoraBerry2022126,_128,_132-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolton201113%E2%80%9314-3) He learned tailoring as an apprentice on [Savile Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savile_Row "Savile Row"), and dressmaking as head designer at French fashion house [Givenchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Givenchy "Givenchy").[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:322-7) Although he worked in [ready-to-wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ready-to-wear "Ready-to-wear") – clothing produced for retail sale – his showpiece designs featured a degree of craftsmanship that verged on _[haute couture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haute\_couture "Haute couture")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:422-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-vogue22-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-menkes2-10)

McQueen's personal fixations had a strong influence on his work. He incorporated his love of animals and the environment throughout his career by using organic materials and making visual references to nature.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012252-12) He was fascinated with [taxidermy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxidermy "Taxidermy"), and owned several pieces, including stuffed [alligator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator "Alligator") heads and a whole [polar bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_bear "Polar bear").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkogh2015180%E2%80%93183-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015316-14) Preserved animals and animal parts had appeared in many previous collections: _[It's a Jungle Out There](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It%27s\_a\_Jungle\_Out\_There\_(collection) "It's a Jungle Out There (collection)")_ (Autumn/Winter 1997) had jackets with horns and crocodile heads, while _[Voss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voss\_(collection) "Voss (collection)")_ (Spring/Summer 2001) featured a dress made with taxidermied hawks positioned as though attacking the model.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkogh2015180%E2%80%93183-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015196-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015312-16)

In the final years of his career, McQueen became increasingly concerned about [human activity damaging the natural world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_impact_on_the_environment "Human impact on the environment").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012252-12)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012187-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18) He felt that humans were beginning to overpower nature and were "in danger of killing the planet through greed", which would lead to the [extinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction "Extinction") of life on earth.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:4-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:3-20) Variations on these ideas formed the basis for his last three completed collections.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012252-12)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012187-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)

Concept and collection
----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Concept and collection")]

[![Image 2: White dress designed by Alexander McQueen, featuring a skull design on the bodice](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Lee_Alexander_McQueen_%26_Ann_Ray_-_Rendez-Vous_15.jpg/250px-Lee_Alexander_McQueen_%26_Ann_Ray_-_Rendez-Vous_15.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lee_Alexander_McQueen_%26_Ann_Ray_-_Rendez-Vous_15.jpg)

Look 7 at _Lee Alexander McQueen & Ann Ray - Rendez-Vous_ (2024)

_Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection_ (Spring/Summer 2009) is the thirty-third collection McQueen made for his eponymous [fashion house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McQueen_(brand) "Alexander McQueen (brand)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox2012138-21) According to the show's program notes, McQueen drew inspiration from the [theory of natural selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_natural_selection "Theory of natural selection") as described by [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin "Charles Darwin") in his seminal 1859 work _[On the Origin of Species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Origin\_of\_Species "On the Origin of Species")_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012187-17)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)_Natural Dis-tinction_ is known for its pioneering use of digital prints, which were engineered to match the [patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern_(sewing) "Pattern (sewing)") of their garments, rather than the usual practice of the pattern being cut to accommodate an existing print.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEsguerraHansen202289-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox201097-24) The collection's prints were derived from natural materials, in the latter half manipulated to appear [kaleidoscopic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaleidoscope "Kaleidoscope").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016276-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEsguerraHansen2022119-26) Two distinct phases of designs contrasted the beauty of nature with the impact of human industry.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012252-12)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)

The first portion of the collection visually referenced unspoiled nature using soft colours, natural materials like leather, delicate embroidery, loose [fringe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fringe_(trim) "Fringe (trim)"), and flowing, organic shapes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012187-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253%E2%80%93255-28) Prints in this section were floral or derived from [wood grain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_grain "Wood grain") in light shades of brown.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253%E2%80%93255-28) Many designs featured embroidered floral motifs or fabric flowers.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016276-25)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012191-29) In some, the flowers were set beneath transparent [tulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulle_(netting) "Tulle (netting)"), evoking imagery of scientific specimens kept beneath glass, as was common in the Victorian era.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18) The skull, by that point a McQueen signature, appeared on the front of a white minidress in Look 7.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012189-30)

In the second half of the collection, inspiration shifted to the industrial and modern, with two contrasting colour schemes. Some designs had patterns in artificially bright colours, while the rest were in shades of black and white. The prints in this section were still mainly derived from nature – flowers, crystals, and bones – but were digitally manipulated to look unnaturally angular and symmetrical.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253%E2%80%93254-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHomer2023112-32) McQueen described the prints as organic in nature but "enhanced, synthetic - touched by man".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:3-20) Other prints were based on buildings like the [Eiffel Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower "Eiffel Tower") or a photograph by [Dan Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Holdsworth "Dan Holdsworth").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253%E2%80%93254-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHomer2023112-32) Artificial and structured textiles predominated: [Lycra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycra "Lycra") for leggings and dresses, and [bonded leather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonded_leather "Bonded leather") dyed black, calling to mind [fetish wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fetish_wear "Fetish wear").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253%E2%80%93255-28) Some dresses and jumpsuits were encrusted with minerals; the final look was a jumpsuit covered with pieces of real [amber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber "Amber").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016276-25)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012192-33)

Across the collection, the silhouettes were both classical and experimental. The garments were designed to fit an antique [Victorian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") mannequin, leading to what [Susannah Frankel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susannah_Frankel "Susannah Frankel") called a "slightly truncated hourglass silhouette".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:3-20) Wearable items like [leggings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leggings "Leggings") and [shift dresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_dress "Shift dress") hinted at McQueen's efforts to keep the collection viable for retail sales.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox201096-34) Despite this, McQueen's characteristic tailoring appeared in precisely-cut minidresses, [frock coats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frock_coat "Frock coat"), and slim [trouser suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trouser_suit "Trouser suit").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox2010100-35) High [Edwardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwardian_era "Edwardian era") collars and [leg-of-mutton sleeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leg-of-mutton_sleeve "Leg-of-mutton sleeve") showcased his ever-present [historicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicism_(art) "Historicism (art)") tendencies, as did designs that appeared to reference _The Tailor's Pattern Book_ (1589) by Spanish mathematician [Juan de Alcega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_Alcega "Juan de Alcega").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012189-30)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHonigman202154-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015313-37)

McQueen had become known for playing with the silhouette by cutting or structuring garments to produce unusual shapes, and he returned to these ideas in _Natural Dis-tinction_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012212,_253-38) The collection's more experimental designs exaggerated the wearer's body beyond natural human proportions, with cinched waists and padded shoulders and hips.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012189-30)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox2010100-35)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilcox201589-39) Intricately folded fabric created coccoon dresses that surrounded the body. Other short dresses had structured, rounded skirts resembling [bell jars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_jar "Bell jar").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilcox201589-39)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016276-25)

[![Image 3: Yellow and white diamond-patterned sheath dress on a stand](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Alexander_McQueen_-_Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection_SS_2009_-_Look_24.jpg/250px-Alexander_McQueen_-_Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection_SS_2009_-_Look_24.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexander_McQueen_-_Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection_SS_2009_-_Look_24.jpg)

Look 24 as presented at _Fashion Fictions_ at the [Vancouver Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Art_Gallery "Vancouver Art Gallery") (2023)

The runway show was staged on 3 October 2008 at the [Cent Quatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent_Quatre "Cent Quatre") building in Paris, a community centre that was once a [mortuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortuary "Mortuary").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016347-40)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22) The invitation featured a [lenticular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenticular_printing "Lenticular printing") portrait of McQueen that transformed into a skull. McQueen's nephew, Gary McQueen, who worked as a menswear assistant with the company, had created the skull image as a print for the menswear line.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2015346-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Neill2015274-42) McQueen decided he wanted to use it instead and had his nephew rework it into the shifting image for the invite.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Neill2015274-42)

McQueen typically worked with a consistent creative team for his shows. Overall styling was handled by [Tabitha Simmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabitha_Simmons "Tabitha Simmons"), while Gainsbury & Whiting were responsible for production.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016347-40) Joseph Bennett, who had designed all of McQueen's runways since [_No. 13_](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=No._13_(Alexander_McQueen_collection)&action=edit&redlink=1 "No. 13 (Alexander McQueen collection) (page does not exist)") (Spring/Summer 1999), returned for [set design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_design "Set design").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-tt-44) Hair was styled by Paul Hanlon, make-up by [Peter Philips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Philips_(make-up_artist) "Peter Philips (make-up artist)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016347-40)

The catwalk was framed by two lines of exotic [taxidermy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxidermy "Taxidermy") animals, including an elephant, giraffe, and several large cats.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012187-17) Accordingly, the show opened with a soundtrack of animal noises – roaring, hoofbeats, and elephant calls – before transitioning to [electronic dance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012189,_192-45) A large round screen at the rear of the stage featured various projections of the Earth, the moon, and the sun, and McQueen's own eyeball.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-tt-44) McQueen's typical runway theatrics were absent.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012192-33)

Models were styled with see-through hairnets used as veils over their heads and faces.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox2012138-21)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012189-30) Author Chloe Fox felt they provided a "foetal sameness" as though the models were freshly-born specimens of a "new breed".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox2012138-21)

Forty-one looks were presented in roughly two phases.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253-46) The first half of the collection featured designs that represented the natural world before human interference. These looks featured lighter colours, floral elements, and prints of wood grain. The phase closed with a trio of minidresses covered with metallic enamel flowers, contrasting the softness of the preceding items.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)

The second half of the show opened with a short series of tailored minidresses in brightly-coloured patterns before transitioning to eveningwear, with leather dresses and tailored patterned looks in monochrome.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253%E2%80%93254-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHomer2023112-32) The final four looks were a series of dresses and jumpsuits encrusted with minerals, including the last jumpsuit, covered with pieces of real [amber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber "Amber").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015320-18)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012192-33) After the models took their final turn, McQueen came out to take his bow in a rabbit [costume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume "Costume").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016276-25)

Look 30 at _Rendez-Vous_

Critical reception for _Natural Dis-tinction_ was somewhat mixed. Anne Slowey of [_Elle_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elle_(magazine) "Elle (magazine)") reported that critical reception for _Natural Dis-tinction_ was "lukewarm", but felt the industry was "charmed" by his appearance in a rabbit suit.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-47)

The environmentalist theme attracted commentary from journalists. Sarah Mower of [_Vogue_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)") and the staff writer for [_Women's Wear Daily_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_Wear_Daily "Women's Wear Daily") (_WWD_) were surprised that it did not lead to the kind of dark, angry collection that McQueen was known for.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:5-48)[Jess Cartner-Morley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jess_Cartner-Morley "Jess Cartner-Morley") of _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ thought the theme was ironic given the use of animal materials in McQueen's designs.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:4-19) In an April 2009 article for [_The Independent_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent "The Independent"), Frankel considered _Natural Dis-tinction_ the most fully-realised exploration of an environmental theme that ran through the entire Spring/Summer 2009 season. She called the collection proof that conceptual fashion no longer needed to "denote heaviness or obvious difficulty", and could still be light and commercially viable.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:3-20)

Critics generally preferred the first half of the collection.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:4-19)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:5-48) The _WWD_ writer felt the first half was "more beautiful" than the latter.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:5-48) Mower was pleased with the romantic execution and highlighted the fringed designs as "two of the season's most sublime".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27) Cartner-Morley felt the best designs were those which balanced "pretty and menacing" elements.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:4-19) Her favourite was Look 2, a minidress which featured yellow silk flowers beneath layers of see-through mesh.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:4-19)

Several critics noted the adherence to McQueen's typical tailored shapes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:4-19)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:5-48) Frankel felt McQueen's workmanship was improving each season, citing his embroidery, fabric choices, and digital prints.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:6-49) Mower thought McQueen's choice to produce a colourful collection with "eased-up tailoring" was intended to promote sales; she felt it would be commercially viable.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:1-27)

Look 16, a brown bodysuit with long patterned coat, attracted commentary for its unusual, inhuman-looking design. [Claire Wilcox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claire_Wilcox "Claire Wilcox") wrote that it "stretched the thorax of the model, suggesting genetic mutation", while Katherine Gleason described the wearer as appearing like "a visiting dignitary from another planet".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012191-29)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox2016276-25) Both [Andrew Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Wilson_(author) "Andrew Wilson (author)") and Judith Watt described the pointed shoulders of the coat as resembling a [manta ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manta_ray "Manta ray").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012254-50)

Some reviewers were disappointed with the lack of runway performance art, which they had come to expect from McQueen.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason2012192-33) Despite this, the _WWD_ reviewer considered the show a strong one with a "stunning" set and called it "among the most intriguing in a lackluster season".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-:5-48)

Despite the mixed contemporary reception, authors have retrospectively considered the collection's ideas intriguing. Wilson felt the clothes presented "the look of an alternative species, something that might have stepped from a space-age [Noah’s Ark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah%27s_Ark "Noah's Ark")."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22) Chloe Fox wrote that the "thoroughly modern looks cemented McQueen’s reputation as a sartorial soothsayer, a man with a passionate commitment to the evolution of fashion".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox2012138-21)

[![Image 5: Dress form wearing a beige dress with floral embellishments](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Lee_Alexander_McQueen_%26_Ann_Ray_-_Rendez-Vous_33.jpg/250px-Lee_Alexander_McQueen_%26_Ann_Ray_-_Rendez-Vous_33.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lee_Alexander_McQueen_%26_Ann_Ray_-_Rendez-Vous_33.jpg)

Look 18, one of the bell jar dresses, at _Rendez-Vous_

Wilson took the rabbit costume as a possible reference to [_Donnie Darko_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donnie_Darko "Donnie Darko") (2001), in which a man in a rabbit suit predicts the end of the world.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22) Watt likened it to the genetically-engineered monster rabbit that causes chaos in the animated film [_Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_%26_Gromit:_The_Curse_of_the_Were-Rabbit "Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit") (2005).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012255-51)

According to O'Neill, McQueen claimed that the skull design was based on the desiccated head of Mrs. Bates seen in the film [_Psycho_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho_(1960_film) "Psycho (1960 film)") (1960), although he notes that this contradicts the actual origin of the image.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-53) O'Neill suggested that the _Psycho_ reference indicated that McQueen was marking the collection as being of an "unnatural order", given the perverse posthumous relationship between Mrs. Bates and her son [Norman Bates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Bates "Norman Bates").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Neill2015274-42) In an essay about McQueen's use of [death symbolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbols_of_death "Symbols of death"), Eleanor Townsend cited the skull image from the _Natural Dis-tinction_ invitation as an example of the designer's awareness of his own mortality.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTETownsend2015159-54)

Fashion journalist Alex Fury argued that _Natural Dis-tinction_ was an example of McQueen expressing his vision "through the bodies of his models" in conjunction with the stripped-down set dressing. The clothing, with its exploration of evolution and nature, is contrasted with the backdrop of the taxidermy animals.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFury2015226-55) Researcher Lisa Skogh noted that McQueen often incorporated concepts and objects which might have appeared in a [cabinet of curiosities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_curiosities "Cabinet of curiosities") – collections of natural and historical objects that were the precursor to modern museum.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkogh2015179-56) She identified the taxidermy animals lining the runway as part of this tradition, likening them to "a re-created [Garden of Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_of_Eden "Garden of Eden")".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkogh2015180%E2%80%93182-57)

McQueen continued to explore the impact of humanity on nature in his next two collections. _[The Horn of Plenty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Horn\_of\_Plenty "The Horn of Plenty")_ (Autumn/Winter 2009) concerned wastefulness in the fashion industry and _[Plato's Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato%27s\_Atlantis "Plato's Atlantis")_ (Spring/Summer 2010), his final completed collection, envisioned a flooded post-[climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") world.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012252-12) Considering the collections in retrospect, Wilcox wrote that _Natural Dis-tinction_ clearly "foreshadowed" its "exceptionally innovative" successor, _Plato's Atlantis_, which had similar dresses with colourful, digitally-worked patterns.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilcox201589-39)

_Natural Dis-tinction_ prompted a trend for printed [Lycra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycra "Lycra") garments such as leggings, which reappeared in his next collections and were imitated by other brands.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnox201098-58) McQueen is credited with popularising the use of digitally-engineered prints in fashion, beginning with this collection.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt2012253-46)_[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural\_Dis-tinction\_Un-natural\_Selection#cite\_note-FOOTNOTEFox2012138-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural\_Dis-tinction\_Un-natural\_Selection#cite\_note-FOOTNOTEEsguerraHansen202289-23)_ He continued to experiment with this novel technique in his remaining collections.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrankel201127-59)

### Museum ownership and exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Museum ownership and exhibitions")]

A pair of shoes from _Natural Dis-tinction_ appeared in _[Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander\_McQueen:\_Savage\_Beauty "Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty")_, a retrospective exhibition of McQueen's designs originally staged at the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art") in 2011. They were placed in the Cabinet of Curiosities section with other accessories.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolton2011235-65) The image from the _Natural Dis-tinction_ invitation, with McQueen's face shifting into a skull, was used for the front cover of the [exhibition catalogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_catalogue "Exhibition catalogue").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015317-22)

Three items owned by the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art") appeared in the museum's exhibition _Lee Alexander McQueen: Mind, Mythos, Muse_, originally staged in 2022: Looks 20 and 32, digitally-printed [minidresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minidress "Minidress"), and a pair of shoes.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEsguerraHansen2022172-66)

When the [National Gallery of Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Victoria "National Gallery of Victoria") (NGV) in Australia restaged _Mind, Mythos, Muse_, they added garments from their own collection: Look 12, a beige printed jacket and skirt set; Look 15, a fringed dress; and Look 22, a blue printed jacket and leggings set.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection#cite_note-71)

3.title: What is natural selection? | Natural History Museum
3.description: Discover what natural selection theory is, how adaptations work, the story of Darwin's finches and whether we are still evolving.
3.content:
Natural selection is a mechanism of evolution. Organisms that are more adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and pass on the genes that aided their success. This process causes species to change and diverge over time.

Natural selection is one of the ways to account for the millions of species that have lived on Earth.

[Charles Darwin](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/charles-darwin-most-famous-biologist.html) (1809-1882) and [Alfred Russel Wallace](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/who-was-alfred-russel-wallace.html) (1823-1913) are jointly credited with coming up with the theory of evolution by natural selection, having co-published on it in 1858. Darwin has generally overshadowed Wallace since the publication of [On the Origin of Species](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/services/library/collections/darwin.html) in 1859, however.

![Image 1: Original editions of Darwin's On the Origin of Species, alongside a modern facsimile](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/Origin-of-Species-editions-two-column.jpg)

The Museum’s Library holds the world's largest concentration of Darwin works, with 478 editions of On the Origin of Species in 38 languages.

In Darwin and Wallace’s time, most believed that organisms were too complex to have natural origins and must have been designed by a transcendent God. Natural selection, however, states that even the most complex organisms occur by totally natural processes.

Our researcher [Professor Adrian Lister](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/departments-and-staff/staff-directory/adrian-lister.html) says, “It’s not that biologists don’t understand that organisms are complex and functional, and it does seem almost miraculous that they exist. We realise that, but we think we’ve found another way of explaining it.”

![Image 2: Side by side black and white photographs of Alfred Russel Wallace and Charles Darwin.](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/darwin-wallace-two-column.jpg)

Wallace (left) and Darwin (right) came up with very similar theories on evolution. Darwin has generally overshadowed Wallace’s contributions, however.

How does natural selection work?
--------------------------------

In natural selection, genetic mutations that are beneficial to an individual’s survival are passed on through reproduction. This results in a new generation of organisms that are more likely to survive to reproduce.

For example, evolving long necks has enabled giraffes to feed on leaves that others can’t reach, giving them a competitive advantage. Thanks to a better food source, those with longer necks were able to survive to reproduce and so pass on the characteristic to the next generation. Those with shorter necks and access to less food would be less likely to survive to pass on their genes.

![Image 3: A wild giraffe feeding from the top branches of a tree.](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/giraffe-tanzania-two-column.jpg)

Adrian explains, “If you took 1,000 giraffes and measured their necks, they’re all going to be slightly different from one another. Those differences are at least in part determined by their genes.”

“The ones with longer necks may leave proportionally more offspring, because they’ve fed better and have maybe been better in competing for mates because they’re stronger. Then, if you were to measure the necks of the next generation, they’re also going to vary, but the average will have shifted slightly towards the longer ones. The process carries on generation after generation.”

What is an adaptation?
----------------------

An adaptation is a physical or behavioural characteristic that helps an organism to survive in its environment.

But not all characteristics of an animal are adaptations.

Adaptations for one purpose can be co-opted for another. For instance, feathers were an adaptation for thermoregulation – their use for flight only came later. This means that feathers are an exaptation for flight, rather than an adaptation.

Adaptations can also become outdated, such as the tough exterior of the calabash fruit, _Crescentia cujete_. This gourd is generally thought to have evolved to avoid being eaten by Gomphotheres, a family of elephant-like animals. But these animals went extinct around 10,000 years ago, so the fruit’s adaptation no longer has a survival benefit.

![Image 4: A tree bearing large, green calabash fruit.](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/calabash-fruit-two-column.jpg)

Selection for adaptation is not the only cause of evolution. For example, [species](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-a-species.html) change can be caused by neutral mutations that have no negative or positive effect on an individual. Change can also occur by genetic drift or gene flow.

What does ‘survival of the fittest’ mean?
-----------------------------------------

In terms of evolution, an animal that is ‘fit’ is one that’s adapted to its environment. This concept is at the core of natural selection, although the term ‘survival of the fittest’ has often been misunderstood and may be best avoided.

There is also a degree of randomness to evolution, so the best-adapted animal won’t always be the one to survive.

Adrian explains, “If you’re going to get hit by a rock or something, it’s just bad luck. But on average and over time, the ones that survive are the ones that are fittest – the ones that have the best adaptations.”

![Image 5: A peppered moth camouflaged against a tree trunk.](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/peppered-moth-camouflage.jpg)

Peppered moths, _Biston betularia_, are difficult to see when they perch on tree bark. Those that blend in best are less likely to be preyed on, so have advantage for survival.

Quick quiz

Which birds inspired Charles Darwin’s natural selection theory?
---------------------------------------------------------------

What are Darwin’s finches?
--------------------------

Darwin [collected many animal specimens](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/charles-darwins-octopus.html) during the voyage of HMS Beagle (1831-1836). Among his best-known are the finches, of which he collected around 14 species from the Galápagos Islands. The birds sit within the same taxonomic family and have a diverse array of beak sizes and shapes. These correspond to both their differing primary food sources and divergence due to isolation on different islands.

The green warbler-finch, _Certhidea olivacea_, for example, has a sharp, slender beak which is perfect for feeding on small insects. In comparison, the large ground finch, _Geospiza magnirostris_, has a short, stocky beak to crack seeds and nuts.

![Image 6: The heads of two Galapagos finch specimens](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/warbler-finch-large-ground-finch-comparison-two-column.jpg)

The Galápagos finches have distinctly different beak shapes and sizes, as can be seen here from specimens of a green warbler-finch (L) and a large ground finch (R).

Darwin’s finches are often thought of as inspiring a ‘eureka moment’, but it was actually mockingbirds that impacted Darwin's thoughts on evolution.

Darwin had collected mockingbirds in South America before travelling to the Galápagos. On the first island, San Cristóbal – then known as Chatham Island – he saw a bird he recognised as a mockingbird. But on nearby Floreana Island he saw that the mockingbirds were considerably different.

Darwin realised that differences between species of mockingbird on the islands were greater than between those he’d seen across the continent. He began contemplating while aboard HMS Beagle, but it took several years before he came up with his theory of evolution by natural selection.

The finches – once they had been identified as different species by the British ornithologist John Gould – became one useful example among the many other animals he saw.

![Image 7: Three of Darwin's mockingbird specimens from the Natural History Museum's collection.](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/darwins-mockingbirds-two-column.jpg)

Charles Darwin collected these three mockingbird specimens during his time on the Galápagos Islands in 1835, during the voyage of HMS Beagle.

The finches are of scientific interest today. For example, [a study of Daphne Major opens in a new window](http://science.sciencemag.org/content/296/5568/707), a volcanic island in the Galápagos archipelago, began in 1972. It found that natural selection has resulted in changes in the beak shape and size of two species of finch: the medium ground finch, _Geospiza fortis_, and common cactus finch, _Geospiza scandens_. Both species’ beaks have been seen to shrink over time, but followed different patterns.

Darwin thought that natural selection progressed slowly and only occurred over a long period of time. This may often be true, but it has been shown that in some cases a [new species can evolve within a lifetime opens in a new window](http://science.sciencemag.org/content/359/6372/224).

For 31 years, scientists studied the survival of a male finch that emigrated from Santa Cruz Island as well as six generations of its descendants on Daphne Major. From the second generation onwards, the birds behaved as a separate species to the others on the island.

![Image 8: A collection of pinned weevil specimens. They are a variety of shapes and colours. ](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/big-beetles/weevil-selection-collection-two-column.jpg)

Natural selection is one of the ways to account for the millions of species on Earth. For example, the beetle family Curculionidae – also known as weevils or snout beetles – is extremely diverse, with an estimated 83,000 species.

What is Lamarckism?
-------------------

Lamarckism was named after the French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829). It is another theory for why living things change over time, but it takes a different approach to natural selection.

Lamarckism proposes that animals acquire characteristics based on use or disuse during their lives, rather than through hard-coded genetic changes.

In Lamarckian theory, giraffes stretch their necks to make them longer. These animals’ offspring would inherit longer necks as a result of their parents’ efforts.

Adrian says, “If you tried to stretch your neck for 10 minutes each morning, then you would probably end up with your neck being a few millimetres longer for a few years. But your children would not inherit it. That’s where this theory fails.”

Are we still evolving?
----------------------

For millennia, the world was viewed as static. The ideas that mountains could rise, and climate and organisms could change didn’t exist. Earth was thought to exist in an optimal form.

But natural selection relies on the fact that the world is constantly changing. Evolution occurs automatically for survival and for millions of years it has been playing catch-up with our dynamic world.

![Image 9: An adult saiga antelope.](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/content/dam/nhm-www/discover/natural-selection/saiga-two-column.jpg)

“Organisms are either adapted enough to survive and reproduce, or they are sub-optimal and the population shrinks. It may even shrink to zero, and that means extinction,” states Adrian.

Scientists have been able to predict natural selection over short terms. But it’s almost impossible to accurately determine its effects in the future due to unpredictable [fluctuations of the environment](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-climate-change-why-does-it-matter.html).

Natural selection implies that if organisms are surviving, they are adapted. But as the environment changes, we may find that what was once an adaptation may no longer be useful.

Although it’s possible for evolution to occur quickly, the more rapidly the planet changes, the harder it is for evolution to keep pace and the more serious the risk of a [massive rise in extinctions](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-mass-extinction-and-are-we-facing-a-sixth-one.html) becomes.
